# Part 1: Analysis of ovarian cancer data

The file `ova.rds` contains data of 358 patients with advanced ovarian cancer, all of which are treated with a similar type of chemotherapy. All patients have been followed for at least 4 years since the start of treatment. The outcome variable (surv) indicates whether the patient has died (surv=0) or is still alive (surv=1) after 4 years of follow-up. 

## Data dictionary of `ova.rds`

```{r}
	myPath <- 'data/ova.rds'	# needs to be changed
	data <- readRDS(myPath)
```

### `time`

Follow-up time measured in days.

### `karn`
Karnovsky-index (a measure for the mobility of the patient, higher is better) at the start of treatment, coded as

| Code  |        Index  |
|------:|--------------:|
|     6 |         <= 60 |
|     7 |  > 60 & <= 70 |
|     8 |  > 70 & <= 80 |
|     9 |  > 80 & <= 90 |
|    10 | > 90 & <= 100 |


### `diam`
The diameter of residual tumor after surgery as determined by microscopy, coded as

| Code  |      Diameter |
|------:|--------------:|
|     0 |         < 1cm |
|     1 |         1-2cm |
|     2 |         2-5cm |
|     3 |         > 5cm |

### `figo`

FIGO status for the invasion of the tumor, either III (`figo` = 0) or IV( `figo` = 1).

### `ascites`

Presence of ascites: 0 "unknown", 1 "absent", 2 "present".

## Learning R

The `ifelse` function can be used to make decisions on whole vectors. `ifelse(a, x, y)` takes three vectors of the same length. The first vector `a` is logical, meaning it contains only values `TRUE` or `FALSE`. `ifelse` iterates the vector `a`. If the values is `TRUE`, `ifelse` returns the value of `x` at the same position, otherwise the value of `y` at that position. As an example, we determine, whether the Karnovsky-index is larger or equal to 8. In the data, the Karnovsky-index is entered as a categorical variable. To convert to an integer, the functions `as.character` and `as.integer` are used.

```{r}
	data$karnI = as.integer(as.character(data$karn))
	karn8 <- ifelse(data$karnI >= 8, 'Larger or equal to 8', 'Smaller than 8')
```

Here is equivalent code that uses `sapply` as introduced in the ANOVA CP.

```{r}
	karn8.1 <- sapply(data$karnI, function(k) if (k >= 8) 'Larger or equal to 8' else 'Smaller than 8')
```

## Q2: Create an outcome variable for patient survival

For a logistic regression, the outcome variable needs to be defined as an event (yes/no). For a clear interpretation, the event should have the same interpretation for all patients. `time` indicates follow-up time which differs between patients. We therefore define our event as death in the first four years of follow-up. For, patients who were alive but followed up for less than 4 years, the event is not defined as the event could have occurred in the remaining time until 4 years.

Create a new variable `y` that records whether patients had en event or not according to the above definition. `y` should be set to `NA` when follow-up was insufficient for survivors.

```{r}
	data$y <- ifelse(data$time/365 >= 4 | data$death == 1, data$death, NA)
```

How many patients got an `NA`? Use the table function with argument `useNA = 'ifany'`.

## Q3: Analyze the influence of `figo` on patient survival

Remove `NA` values for `y` from the data set.

```{r}
	data <- data[!is.na(data$y), ]
```

Calculate a Chisquare test for the variables `y` and `figo`. Both `chisq.test` and `fisher.test` can be used. As `fisher.test` also calculates the OR together wiht a confidence interval, `fisher.test` is preferred in this CP.

**fillin**:  

Use a logistic regression for the same analysis. function `glm(outcome ~ covariate, data, family = binomial()` has to be used (replacint `outcome`, `covariate`). Use the `summary` function to get a regression table.

```{r}
	logRegFigo <- glm(y ~ figo, data, family = binomial())
	print(summary(logRegFigo))
```

Calculate the OR of `figo` for the logistic regression and compare with the output of `fisher.test`.

## Q4: Analyze the influence of `karn` on patient survival

The `karn` variable is categorical in the data set. For this analysis, we want to treat is as a numeric variable. Use `as.numeric` to change the data type of `karn`.

```{r}
	data$karn <- as.numeric(data$karn)
```

Create a histogram, comparing survivors and non-survivors.

```{r}
	ggplot(data, aes(x = karn, fill = as.factor(death))) +
		geom_histogram(position = position_dodge(), bins = 5) +
		theme_bw()
```

To better show differences, the next plot uses proportions instead of counts.
```{r}
	ggplot(data, aes(x = karn, fill = as.factor(death))) + geom_bar(aes(y = ..prop.., group = as.factor(death)), position = position_dodge()) + theme_bw()
```

Use a logistic regression to analyze the influence of `karn` on `y`. Interpret your result. Is the result expected?

# Q6: Analyze the variables `karn`, `figo`, `broders`, `ascites`, `diam`

Perform logistic regrssions for the variables listed above (`karn` and `figo` are included again for easy comparison). Analyzing variables one-by-one is called a marginal analysis.

```{r}
	summary(glm(y ~ karn, data, family = binomial()))
	summary(glm(y ~ figo, data, family = binomial()))
	summary(glm(y ~ broders, data, family = binomial()))
	summary(glm(y ~ ascites, data, family = binomial()))
	summary(glm(y ~ diam, data, family = binomial()))
```

Interpret the result for `ascites`.

**fillin**:  

For which variables are regression coefficients significantly different from zero at an alpha-level of 0.05 (except for the intercept)?

**fillin**:  

Do you believe that some of the variables are correlated? Give examples and support these with arguments.

**fillin**:  

If variables are correlated any effect seen in a regression could be an indirect effect of one of the variables only. An effect in a given variable might only be seen because the variable is correlated with another variable which has a true effect. To separate the effect of such variables all of them have to be included in the regression model. Repeat the logistic regression using all variables identified as significant above (use `y ~ cov1 + cov2 + ...` for the formula). This is called a multivariate analysis.

**fillin**:  

Which differences do you see? What is your interpretation?
